paper.citation: Mendoza Barrios M, Deconinck E, Vanhee C, Lamme EK, 't Hart-Bakker I, Syversen PV, et al. SARMs, Metabolic Modulators and Growth Hormone Secretagogues in Suspected Illegal Medicines, Bought as Sport Performance Enhancers: A Retro- and Prospective Study Within the GEON. Drug Testing and Analysis. 2025.
paper.abstract: Market-surveillance study by European and partner OMCL laboratories of suspected illegal products containing SARMs, metabolic modulators or growth hormone secretagogues, sold as sport performance enhancers.
paper.tldr: Illegal products containing SARMs and related drugs are sold for sport performance, often labelled as medicines or sold as supplements. Products from unregulated sources can contain unapproved drugs, sometimes unlabelled or at very high doses.
paper.methods: OMCL laboratories collected retrospective and prospective data from January 2018 to September 2023 using a harmonised reporting template, with mainly LC-MS screening. Results were summarised as counts by origin, product type, dosage form, molecule and quantity.
paper.findings: Of 336 reported samples, 12 had no in-scope active compound, leaving 324 samples; samples with more than one target compound gave 354 valid results. About 86% of samples came from the illegal supply chain, 65% of results were presented as medicines and 24% as dietary supplements. Eighteen molecules were detected, led by ibutamoren (62 reports), ligandrol (48), ostarine (46), cardarine (45) and andarine (34).
paper.limitations: Only OMCL results were counted, so the number of circulating products is higher. Quantitative data were limited and reported in mixed units. Health outcomes in consumers were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Products labelled as medicines or supplements can contain unapproved SARMs or other drugs, and dosing varied widely, including very high-dose liquids and high-purity powders for self-dosing. The authors advise against buying these products from suspected websites that hide a physical address.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Unregulated products marketed for muscle gain or performance often lack ingredient labels and vary widely in dose. The study did not assess any performance effect.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it describes product contents and does not assess injury, recovery or clinical outcomes in athletes.

records.sourceFile: Social media may cause emergent SARMs abuse by athletes - A content quality analysis of the most popular YouTube videos.pdf

paper.citation: Vasireddi N, Hahamyan HA, Kumar Y, Ng MK, Voos JE, Calcei JG. Social Media May Cause Emergent SARMs Abuse by Athletes: A Content Quality Analysis of the Most Popular YouTube Videos. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Objectives: To analyse the quality, educational content and reliability of the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs. Methods: On 28 November 2021 the top 100 videos for 'SARMs' were coded for source, content category, JAMA reliability score, Global Quality Score (GQS), attitude toward SARMs and cycle advice. Results: Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 of 4 and mean GQS was 2.5 ± 1.1 of 5; patient videos had lower GQS than athletic trainer videos. Conclusion: Quality and reliability were low, and the authors argue that social media likely contributes to SARMs abuse.
paper.tldr: The most viewed YouTube videos on SARMs were of low quality and reliability, and nearly half gave cycle advice. Staff should expect athletes to meet this content and be ready to correct it, but the study does not show that it causes drug use.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the first 100 YouTube videos for 'SARMs' in relevance order. Two authors independently scored each video for uploader type, content category, JAMA reliability (0 to 4), Global Quality Score (1 to 5), attitude toward SARMs and specific cycle or dosing support, and descriptive and regression statistics were used.
paper.findings: Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 and mean GQS was 2.5 ± 1.1, with patient videos scoring lower than athletic trainer videos (2.11 vs 2.95, p < 0.01). Forty-seven percent of videos gave cycle help, and 40% took a positive attitude toward SARMs use. Videos averaged 147,994 views each.
paper.limitations: Only 100 videos from a single search on one date, on one platform. Intraobserver variability was not measured, no video was linked to measured SARMs use, and the 'athletic trainer' source group included anyone with athletic training or coaching credentials. The authors' statement that social media likely causes abuse is not tested by the data.
paper.practicalImplications: When athletes raise SARMs content, expect low-quality material, and note that nearly half of it gives cycle advice without clinical support. Point athletes to reliable sources and discuss the harms; the study does not show that any video changes behaviour.
paper.athleteDev: Much of the online SARMs information athletes see is low quality, and some of it is positive about use. The study does not measure performance effects, dosing outcomes or use rates among athletes.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. It analyses YouTube videos rather than injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Postion Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol).pdf

paper.citation: Pillay L, Thompson C, Tabane C, Kirby J, Hendricks S, Swart J, et al. South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Position Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol). S Afr J Sports Med. 2023;35(1):1-4.
paper.abstract: Unlabelled opening paragraph: CBD and THC have become easily available to athletes. Using them may expose an athlete to an adverse analytical finding (a positive test) and sanction, especially without a therapeutic use exemption. The statement aims to clarify the use of CBD and THC and their anti-doping risks, and the South African Sports Medicine Association supports it.
paper.tldr: CBD is not prohibited, but THC is, and a CBD product can contain enough THC to cause a positive test. Athletes should check every product against the Prohibited List and obtain a therapeutic use exemption before any medical use of a THC-containing product.
paper.methods: Position statement by a national anti-doping body, supported by the national sports medicine association. It reviews WADA rules, South African law, product types and the evidence base, with no original data and no described search method.
paper.findings: CBD is not on the Prohibited List, while cannabis (THC) is prohibited in competition. WADA's 2022 expert group concluded that THC meets the criteria for the List because it is a health risk, mainly neurological, and its in-competition use violates the spirit of sport; it found no objective evidence of physiological performance enhancement but could not exclude neuropsychological enhancement. The urine threshold for an adverse analytical finding is 150 ng/ml, and 180 ng/ml triggers sanction. The statement adds that evidence for CBD and THC in anxiety, pain, sleep disorders and chemotherapy side effects is low in quality.
paper.limitations: Position statement with no described search method or evidence grading, and the cited studies are mostly small or uncontrolled. It presents an anti-doping viewpoint, and the statement itself says South African cannabis legislation is still being approved in stages. The authors declare no conflicts of interest or funding.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes who use CBD should check each product, since some contain THC and a single positive test can bring sanctions. Medical use of a THC-containing product for a diagnosed condition needs a therapeutic use exemption before treatment starts, and evidence-based first-line options should be tried first.
paper.athleteDev: THC is banned in competition, and WADA's 2022 group found no objective evidence that it enhances physical performance, although neuropsychological effects cannot be excluded. Staff should not treat THC as a performance aid, and should ask about CBD use because its THC content is a doping risk.
paper.rtp: Limited return-to-sport value because it sets no return-to-play rules. It is relevant only where cannabinoids are used for pain, sleep or nausea during rehabilitation, where a THC-containing product needs a therapeutic use exemption.

records.sourceFile: Sport and exercise genomics - The FIMS 2019 consensus statement update.pdf

paper.citation: Tanisawa K, Wang G, Seto J, Verdouka I, Twycross-Lewis R, Karanikolou A, et al. Sport and exercise genomics: the FIMS 2019 consensus statement update. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (epub ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Updates a previous consensus on sport and exercise genomics using a SWOT analysis and develops a guiding reference covering the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of the field, with emphasis on ethics, data protection and athlete privacy.
paper.tldr: Genetic information from athletes has real potential, but most sport genetic findings are unreplicated. The guidance calls for replication studies, privacy safeguards and genetic counselling before genetic information is used for athletes.
paper.methods: Consensus update built on a SWOT analysis. No sample, search protocol or formal voting method is reported.
paper.findings: The authors state that most sport and exercise gene associations have not been replicated, that polygenic traits need very large samples (about 5,500 cases and as many controls to detect an odds ratio of 1.2 in a case-control GWAS), and that genetic testing may help evaluate athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease. They list threats including re-identification of anonymised genotype data, inaccurate testing based on thin evidence, discrimination and gene doping.
paper.limitations: The statement is an expert guidance document rather than an evidence synthesis, and the consensus process is not described. The authors acknowledge small samples and limited replication in the field, and say the guidance will be updated as evidence emerges.
paper.practicalImplications: Before collecting athlete genetic data, plan consent, data protection and genetic counselling for results that could be misread. Treat sport genetic findings as research hypotheses until they are replicated.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The guidance does not support using genetic markers to select sports or set training. It says that selecting sports from a few variants is unlikely to be possible because athletic performance is polygenic.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The statement does not address return to play. Its genetic-testing remarks concern evaluating athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease.

records.sourceFile: Sport-related injury and performance enhancing substance use by young athletes.pdf

paper.citation: McNaughton M, Hunt D, Parmeter B, O'Brien M, Cook D, Meehan W, et al. Sport-Related Injury and Performance Enhancing Substance Use by Young Athletes. Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Compares legal performance enhancing substance (PES) use and consideration of banned PES use in young athletes aged 6 to 25 with a season-ending injury, concussion, non-season-ending injury or no injury, using a cross-sectional dataset from 2013 to 2020. The authors found no association between injury group and PES use after adjustment, and identify male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability as factors linked to PES use.
paper.tldr: Among young athletes at an injury prevention clinic, 14% reported legal PES use and 3% considered banned PES. Injury status was not associated with either after adjustment; male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability were.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional analysis of an existing dataset from an injury prevention evaluation (April 2013 to March 2020). Athletes completed an electronic questionnaire covering PES use, injury history, sport contact level and other factors. Multivariable logistic regression used injury group as the exposure, with unadjusted and adjusted models.
paper.findings: Of 952 athletes, 133 had a season-ending injury, 441 a non-season-ending injury, 85 a concussion and 293 no injury. Legal PES use was reported by 136 (14%) and consideration of banned PES use by 28 (3%). Unadjusted, season-ending injury versus no injury gave OR 2.74 for legal PES use and OR 4.01 (95% CI 1.15 to 13.96) for banned PES consideration. In the adjusted models, injury groups were not associated with legal PES use (season-ending injury OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.95). Male sex (OR 1.38), depression history (OR 3.01), weight training (OR 1.66) and belief that weight affects athletic ability (OR 1.75) were associated with legal PES use. Older age (OR 1.18) and male sex (OR 1.57) were associated with banned PES consideration.
paper.limitations: Self-report may under-report PES use, and the authors could not determine whether PES use began before or after injury. The sample is one clinic's population with a wide age range and regional limits. The abstract's statement of no association refers to adjusted models; the unadjusted injury associations were significant. The text gives 954 athletes after exclusions while the tables use 952. The questionnaire offered only male or female sex options when it was designed.
paper.practicalImplications: When seeing young athletes for injury prevention, ask about legal supplement use and weight-related beliefs, and give extra attention to the male, depression and weight-training flags reported here. Do not assume that an injured young athlete is more likely to use PES, because the adjusted analysis did not show this.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: For young athletes who weight train or believe weight affects performance, coaches and clinicians can review supplement use and education needs. The study does not show that these practices improve performance or safety.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not support a PES-based change to return-to-play care, because injury status was not associated with PES use after adjustment. It cannot show whether PES use affects recovery.
